speaker_label: TONY COX, host
text: It's the fourth day of Kwanzaa, the weeklong black American celebration      of community and family.  NPR's Farai Chideya spoke with a writer about      one important thing Kwanzaa shares with other holidays this time of year.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA reporting
text: It's hard to find a holiday that doesn't have food as a centerpiece.  The      African-American celebration Kwanzaa is no exception.  Here to give us a      rundown of Kwanzaa feast is journalist and author Eric Copage.  His      latest book is "Fruits of the Harvest:  Recipes to Celebrate Kwanzaa and      Other Holidays."

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA reporting
text: Hi, Eric.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Hey, Farai.  How are      you?

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: I'm doing great.  So let's talk about Kwanzaa.  First, just      describe a little bit about what this holiday is and how widely it's      celebrated.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Well, celebrated not just around the country but around the      world, too.  It's not a religious holiday; it's a cultural holiday.  It's      a seven-day holiday that begins the day after Christmas and goes until      the new year.

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: So let's talk specifically about this book.  You've written      other books about Kwanzaa.  You're very much steeped in the tradition.      But "Fruits of the Harvest" is really a book of food and remembrance.      What sorts of foods show up on a Kwanzaa table?

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Well, there are all kinds of foods from the African diaspora      that show up on a Kwanzaa table.  And while this book is on one level      kind of focused on Kwanzaa, it's also for other holidays, too, and also      for everyday cooking.  Basically what you do is use something from either      your tradition or from the tradition of the African diaspora.  So for      instance, there's a Piri-Piri shrimp recipe by a woman, and she did      it--one is that recipe comes from Angola.  But the reason she uses it is      to remember her heritage comes from the black fishermen of Long Island.      And a lot of that knowledge has been lost over the years, and so a way of      keeping that alive.

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: What other sorts of traditions, either from the US      African-American traditions or from the African diaspora, show up in your      food--in this book?

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Well, of course, there's fried chicken.  There's a delicious      fried chicken recipe, which I like a lot.  There's a peanut soup recipe,      which of course, comes from the--from West Africa.  But also in my book,      there's recipes from the Tuskegee Institute for sweet potato bread with      raisins and walnuts and a couple of other things.  And the important      thing about that, of course, is that George Washington Carver exercised a      huge influence over that at one point.  And they had these bulletins come      out on different ways you can exploit various kinds of foods:  yams,      peanuts, of course, tomatoes and so on and so forth.  Very full, very      interesting.

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: Yeah, so some of the research, the historical research that      went into black food can resonate today.  So along those lines, let me      ask about historical use of African diaspora food in use today.  In the      past, in the far past, when African-Americans were enslaved or even as      free people didn't have a lot of resources often, people didn't eat much      meat.  But then, of course, as we grew richer, our diet grew richer, and      now a lot of us have diabetes or pre-diabetes.  What about the health      aspects of the recipes in this book?  Are these suitable for people who      might have diabetes or high blood pressure?

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Well, yes, because there are a wide span of recipes in the      book. Some include exotic ingredients such as goat, rabbit and conch.      And then also there are some more common--fish, chicken and beef.  There      are also healthy vegetarian recipes.  There's a vegetarian droloff(ph)      recipe.  The person who gave me the recipe included lots and lots of      different vegetables.

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: And finally, let me just ask you about what the food in a      celebration like Kwanzaa represents.  Holiday celebrations of many faiths      and many cultures really use food to anchor family and friends coming      together. How does the emotional level of food relate to the holiday of      Kwanzaa?

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Well, of course, it's in gathering of the people and that      is, of course, how Dr. Karenga, who created Kwanzaa, meant it to be.  And      when you focus also on the symbolic meaning of the meals, one of the      things I'm most proud about in the book is not only the messages of black      pride, resourcefulness that are conveyed through the 125 recipes, but      also the 75 proverbs and folk tales and snippets of biographies and      autobiographies from people such as Berry Gordy Jr. and Malcolm X and      Fannie Lou Hamer.  And this is an important aspect for Kwanzaa because,      of course, it's a time where we in a sense kind of like reignite our      black pride and take stock of it, of how we've used this black pride in      the previous year and how we pledge to use it in the coming year.

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: That's a great note to leave us with.  Eric Copage is a      best-selling author and an occasional commentator for this program.  His      latest book is "Fruits of the Harvest:  Recipes to Celebrate Kwanzaa and      Other Holidays."

speaker_label: CHIDEYA
text: Happy Kwanzaa, Eric.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, "Fruits of the Harvest")
text: Happy Kwanzaa to you.

speaker_label: TONY COX, host
text: That was NPR's Farai Chideya.

speaker_label: TONY COX, host
text: Thanks for joining us.  That's our program for today.  To listen to this      show, visit npr.org.  NEWS & NOTES was created by NPR News and the      African-American Public Radio Consortium.

speaker_label: TONY COX, host
text: I'm Tony Cox.  This is NEWS & NOTES.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Let's face it brothers and sisters, life is all about getting laid.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Commentator Eric Copage offers his thoughts on the future of black romantic relationships.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: For men, that means monopolizing as many women as possible. For women, it means allying herself with men who can provide the most protection, social advantage and material benefits of her children.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: These (unintelligible) came to mind to recently while I was watching a DVD of the romantic comedy Something New. The film is a sweet tale of an interracial relationship between a successful, beautiful, black lawyer and a successful, handsome, white landscape architect.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: The movie is one of a number of white man, black woman romantic couplings that have become more and more common on both the big and small screen since the beginning of the present century.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Notable movies included Guess Who with Zoe Saldana and Ashton Kutcher, The Rundown with Rosario Dawson and Sean William Scott, and Die Another Day with Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan. Some listeners are probably thinking black men have been involved with white women so it's about time that black women can find a husband and some happiness.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: But something more is at stake. Remember what I said at the beginning and what is regarded as true by anthropologists. There are hard-wired biological forces spurring women to look for good providers, social prestige and protection in their mates.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: White men obviously have more overall social prestige than black men and demonstrably have more money. Salaries aside, centuries of industrial-strength racism have insured that most white men will inherit more money from their parents than the average black American man.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Considering these facts, why wouldn't a black woman choose a white man over a strapping black man who can't successfully flag down a cab at night? Why wouldn't a white man who looks like the Pillsbury Doughboy use his status and earning potential to cherry pick from among the pool of available black women? And why wouldn't a black woman respond to his advances?

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Does this mean that black women should adhere themselves to black men and vice versa out of racial loyalty? That's probably not likely even if it were desirable. First, for African-Americans between the ages of 20 and 39, the prime ages for establishing a household, there are about 11 black women alive for every 10 black men. Besides, in a world where racial barriers to romance is slowly crumbling, common interests are likely to play a larger and larger part in choosing a mate. As the filmmaker and comedian Woody Allen famously said, the heart wants what it wants.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Black women marrying white men in droves is unlikely to happen overnight. According to the 2000 U.S. census, of the six percent of all marriages that are black-white interracial, about 75 percent are between black men and white women. That number has been fairly consistent since 1980. But that latest reliable census datum came before onscreen validation of such relationships, not to mention the merit of other transformations in our rapidly changing society.

speaker_label: Mr. ERIC COPAGE (Author, Black Pearls: meditations, Affirmations, and Inspirations for African Americans)
text: Throughout American history, white men have been apoplectic in their fear of black men taking their women. But present logic suggests that it will be the other way around. Since desegregation we African-Americans have lost ownership of many of our banks, our insurance companies and much of our media. The question with this most intimate phase of desegregation is whether black men and black women are in peril of losing each other.

speaker_label: FARAI CHIDEYA, host
text: Eric Copage is the author of Black Pearls: Meditations, Affirmations and Inspirations for African-Americans.
